title: Statistical Thinking & Descriptive Analytics
excerpt: Start with a clear question, a well-defined group, and a careful look at the data. Learn how averages, spread, charts and unusual values describe what happened—without confusing description with explanation or cause.
objectives: Distinguish a population, sample, parameter and statistic.
Choose summaries and visualizations that match data type, units and distribution.
Calculate and interpret center, spread, quantiles and changes in finance.
Separate description, association, prediction, causality, uncertainty and practical importance.

lessons.title: Start with the question, unit and sample
lessons.body:
Begin by naming the population: all daily 10-year Treasury yield changes in a stated period, for example. The observed subset is the sample. A parameter describes the population; a statistic describes the sample and estimates that parameter. A large sample is not automatically representative: missing crisis days, delisted firms or nonresponding accounts can create selection bias. Record each observation's unit, timestamp, source, definition and missing-value rule before calculating or communicating results. In a teaching example, label numbers as illustrative or simulated rather than implying an invented historical dataset. Random sampling supports generalization, while random assignment supports causal comparisons; they solve different problems.

A small example separates a sample from the population. Suppose a town wants the average weekly energy bill for all 10,000 households, but first calculates the mean from five bills: £40, £50, £60, £70 and £80. Their sample mean is (£40 + £50 + £60 + £70 + £80) ÷ 5 = £60 per week. That £60 describes those five households and is an estimate of the town-wide average—not a fact about every household. A larger sample can make random error smaller, but it still needs a sensible route into the sample.

Ask how the five households were chosen. A random sample drawn from a complete household list can support a town-wide description under its design; five online volunteers may not, even if their arithmetic is perfect. Random sampling helps decide whom the evidence represents. Random assignment instead decides who receives a programme and can support a causal comparison. They solve different problems. See “Penn State STAT 200 — Descriptive Statistics” in the linked sources for a fuller introduction.

Suppose a researcher asks, ‘What was the typical monthly transport cost per household in March 2026?’ The unit is pounds per household per month, not pounds per person. In an illustrative synthetic sample of four households, costs are £90, £110, £130 and £170, so the sample mean is (£90 + £110 + £130 + £170) ÷ 4 = £500 ÷ 4 = £125 per household per month. This statistic describes the sampled households; it does not establish the population mean if renters, rural households or nonrespondents were missed. A sampling frame should define eligible households and the date window before collection. Random sampling can support generalization, but it cannot remove measurement error or guarantee a causal interpretation. For a fuller treatment, see ‘OpenIntro Statistics — Ch. 1: Introduction to Data (CC BY-SA 3.0)’ in the linked sources.

When a sample deliberately overrepresents a subgroup, the plain mean can answer the wrong population question. Suppose an illustrative synthetic survey samples 30 salaried and 30 self-employed households to estimate monthly disposable income, even though the target population is 80% salaried and 20% self-employed. If the within-group sample means are £2,400 and £3,000 per household per month, the unweighted mean is (£2,400 + £3,000) ÷ 2 = £2,700 per household per month. A population-share-weighted estimate is (0.80 × £2,400) + (0.20 × £3,000) = £1,920 + £600 = £2,520 per household per month. The £180 difference is not a calculation error: it reflects the sample’s 50:50 composition versus the population’s 80:20 composition. This correction is descriptive, not causal, and it relies on accurate population shares plus representative measurements within each group. If self-employed households with missing income records differ systematically from respondents, weighting alone will not remove nonresponse or measurement bias. Report both the target population and the weighting rule so readers know which estimand the summary addresses.
lessons.formula: Sample statistic x̄ = (Σxᵢ) / n, where xᵢ is observation i and n is sample size.
lessons.takeaway: A precise question and defensible process matter more than a large row count.

practice.question: You want to describe monthly fund returns but your file contains only funds that survived to today. What limitation should you report first?
practice.hint: Ask which relevant units are systematically absent.
practice.solution: This is survivorship or selection bias: the sample may omit failed or closed funds, so its average need not represent all funds that existed. More rows would not repair the design problem.

lessons.title: Match variable type to a useful display
lessons.body:
Classify the variable before choosing arithmetic. Categorical data are labels, such as sector; ordered categories have rank but not necessarily equal spacing. Quantitative data have meaningful numerical magnitudes, such as a return in percent or a yield in percentage points. Use counts or proportions for categories, and histograms, dot plots or box plots for quantitative observations. A line chart preserves time order and can reveal trends or changing regimes over the measurement window. Always label whether a value is a percent, decimal return, currency amount or percentage-point change, and keep the denominator explicit; 1% and 1 percentage point are not interchangeable in every context.

Illustrative synthetic example (January–June 2025): a local economic office records one weekly grocery bill for each of 12 households, in pounds, and each household’s tenancy type. Grocery spending is quantitative, so group the bills into £40–59 (4 households), £60–79 (5), and £80–99 (3), then draw a histogram with spending in pounds on the horizontal axis and household count on the vertical axis. The five households in the middle bin represent 5 ÷ 12 = 41.7% of this small sample. Tenancy type is categorical, so show its counts or proportions in a bar chart rather than placing labels on a numerical axis. The displays describe this six-month snapshot; they do not turn the categories into measured quantities.

A histogram or bar chart can reveal concentration, skew or group composition in the recorded sample, but it cannot establish that tenancy type causes higher grocery spending, nor that these 12 households represent every household in the area. Before choosing a display, check that each row refers to the same time unit and household, that pounds are defined consistently, and that the denominator for every proportion is stated; if bills are repeated weekly observations, account for that dependence rather than treating them as 12 independent households. Do not read a histogram bar’s height as a probability unless it has been normalized and the bin widths are comparable. The linked source “NIST/SEMATECH — Histogram and exploratory data analysis” gives further guidance.

Imagine an illustrative synthetic survey of 20 small businesses recording payment method and invoice amount in euros. Payment method has counts: bank transfer 12, card 5 and cash 3; the proportions are 12 ÷ 20 = 60%, 5 ÷ 20 = 25% and 3 ÷ 20 = 15%, so a bar chart suits the categories. Invoice amount is quantitative: if six selected invoices are €40, €40, €60, €80, €80 and €200, a dot plot makes the repeated €40 and €80 values visible, while a histogram can show the long right tail. These displays summarize the recorded invoices, not all businesses. The €200 value may be genuine, so do not delete it merely to make the chart symmetrical. For a fuller treatment, see ‘NIST/SEMATECH — Histogram and exploratory data analysis’ in the linked sources.

Use the descriptive lab as a sensitivity check. Illustrative synthetic calculation: with the lab’s 21 fixed daily yield changes plus a shock day set to +8 pp, the 22-observation total is −5.4 pp, so the mean is −5.4 ÷ 22 = −0.245 pp (about −0.25 pp); the ordered middle pair is −0.4 and −0.2 pp, giving a median of (−0.4 + −0.2) ÷ 2 = −0.30 pp. Move only that shock from +8 pp to +18 pp: the total rises by 10 pp, so the mean rises by 10 ÷ 22 = 0.455 pp, to about +0.21 pp, while the median remains −0.30 pp because the shock stays above the central observations. This diagnostic shows how one tail value can change the mean’s sign even when the typical observation, represented here by the median, is unchanged. The calculation assumes each row is one comparable daily change; it is not evidence about actual Treasury yields. In a real series, investigate whether an extreme value is a valid market observation, a unit error, or a data problem before choosing a robust summary or omitting it.
lessons.takeaway: A chart is an argument about what is being measured, so make type, units and order visible.

practice.question: Which display best shows the distribution of 60 simulated monthly returns, and which best shows their order through time?
practice.hint: One question asks about shape; the other asks about sequence.
practice.solution: Use a histogram or dot plot for distribution shape and a time-ordered line chart for sequence, trends and possible regime changes. A single chart cannot answer both questions equally well.

lessons.title: Compare center and spread with a worked example
lessons.body:
Consider six illustrative daily changes in a yield, measured in percentage points: −0.02, −0.01, 0.00, 0.01, 0.02 and 0.10. Their mean is 0.10 ÷ 6 = 0.0167 percentage points, while the median is (0.00 + 0.01) ÷ 2 = 0.005 percentage points. The shock day pulls the mean upward. The sample standard deviation is about 0.0432 percentage points, using s = √[Σ(xᵢ − x̄)²/(n−1)], where xᵢ is a change, x̄ the sample mean and n the count. Report both center and spread, and investigate an extreme value rather than deleting it automatically.

For an illustrative synthetic set of five weekly sales changes, measured in percent, use −2%, 0%, 1%, 1% and 10%. The mean is (−2 + 0 + 1 + 1 + 10) ÷ 5 = 10 ÷ 5 = 2%, while the median is 1% after ordering the values. The range is 10% − (−2%) = 12 percentage points, showing the total span. Here, the 10% week raises the mean above four of the five observations, so the median may better represent a typical week. However, the median can hide how far an extreme lies from the rest, and the range depends on two observations. These summaries describe sales changes; they do not explain why the 10% week occurred or prove a promotion caused it. For a fuller treatment, see ‘OpenIntro Statistics — Ch. 2: Summarizing Data (CC BY-SA 3.0)’ in the linked sources.

A useful robustness check is to calculate how the mean changes when the shock control moves, rather than treating one setting as definitive. Using the lab’s 21 fixed synthetic daily changes, their sum is −13.4 percentage points. With an illustrative shock of +8 pp, the 22-observation mean is (−13.4 + 8) ÷ 22 = −5.4 ÷ 22 = −0.245 pp, whereas raising that shock to +18 pp gives (−13.4 + 18) ÷ 22 = 4.6 ÷ 22 = 0.209 pp. The mean therefore rises by 0.454 pp, exactly 10 pp ÷ 22, because only one observation changed while the denominator stayed 22. In both settings, the median remains −0.4 pp: the shock is still above the middle ordered observations, so it does not cross the center. This contrast is a sensitivity diagnostic, not evidence that either value is erroneous. For observed data, check the timestamp, units, and recording process; if the movement is a genuine market event, retain it and report how much conclusions depend on it. These values are synthetic illustrations, not observed yields.
lessons.formula: s = √[Σ(xᵢ − x̄)²/(n−1)], where s is sample standard deviation.
lessons.takeaway: Mean and standard deviation use every value; median is more resistant when a shock dominates.

practice.question: For the six changes above, which center better describes a typical non-shock day: 0.0167 or 0.005 percentage points?
practice.hint: Compare each candidate with the five ordinary-looking observations and the one shock.
practice.solution: The median, 0.005 percentage points, is more representative of the central observations because the 0.10 shock strongly raises the mean. Neither summary explains why the shock occurred.

lessons.title: Use quantiles and robust summaries
lessons.body:
Quantiles locate positions in an ordered sample. The 25th percentile is Q1, the 50th is the median, and the 75th is Q3. The interquartile range is IQR = Q3 − Q1, describing the middle half in the chosen units. Different software uses slightly different interpolation rules, so document the convention used for small samples and tied values. For skewed returns or yield changes, median and IQR can be more stable descriptions than mean and standard deviation, while percentiles such as the 5th and 95th show tail cutoffs. A percentile is descriptive, not a guaranteed worst-case boundary or probability forecast for future observations.

Consider eight illustrative synthetic delivery times in minutes, already ordered: 12, 14, 15, 16, 18, 20, 45 and 50. Using the median-of-halves convention, the median is (16 + 18) ÷ 2 = 17 minutes. The lower half gives Q1 = (14 + 15) ÷ 2 = 14.5 minutes, and the upper half gives Q3 = (20 + 45) ÷ 2 = 32.5 minutes. Therefore IQR = Q3 − Q1 = 32.5 − 14.5 = 18 minutes, describing the middle 50% under this convention. The 45- and 50-minute deliveries make the distribution right-skewed, so the median and IQR may communicate a typical delivery better than the mean and standard deviation. Quantiles are not guarantees about future maximum delays, and another interpolation rule may give slightly different values. For a fuller treatment, see ‘OpenIntro Statistics — Ch. 2: Summarizing Data (CC BY-SA 3.0)’ in the linked sources.

Suppose an analyst screens ten illustrative synthetic monthly real-wage growth rates, already ordered: −3.0%, −1.2%, −0.8%, −0.4%, 0.1%, 0.3%, 0.5%, 0.7%, 1.0% and 4.0%. Using the median-of-halves convention, the median is (0.1% + 0.3%) ÷ 2 = 0.2%. Q1 is −0.8% (the middle value of the lower five), and Q3 is 0.7% (the middle value of the upper five), so IQR = 0.7 − (−0.8) = 1.5 percentage points. A Tukey screening rule gives a lower fence of −0.8 − 1.5(1.5) = −3.05% and an upper fence of 0.7 + 1.5(1.5) = 2.95%; therefore 4.0% is flagged, while −3.0% is just inside the fence. The arithmetic mean is 0.12% [(sum 1.2%) ÷ 10], close to but below the median because the positive and negative extremes offset. The next step is to check the 4.0% month for a documented measurement or economic event, not delete it automatically. These are synthetic values, and a small sample makes fences unstable; the rule is a screening device, not a claim that the month is erroneous or that future growth cannot exceed 2.95%.
lessons.formula: IQR = Q3 − Q1, where Q1 and Q3 are the 25th and 75th percentiles.
lessons.takeaway: Quantiles expose the middle and tails without letting one extreme observation determine a summary.

lessons.title: Transform levels into meaningful changes
lessons.body:
A price or yield level answers a different question from its change. For a price Pₜ at time t, a simple return is Rₜ = Pₜ/Pₜ₋₁ − 1; this is a decimal proportion, so 0.02 means 2%. A yield change is often reported in percentage points. Aggregating daily observations to monthly values can smooth short-lived moves while hiding their timing. A visible trend, cluster or correlation is an association in the observed data. It may help prediction under testing, but it does not by itself identify a cause. State the transformation, frequency, horizon and assumptions before interpreting a pattern.

Suppose an illustrative synthetic asset has prices of $80 at Monday’s close, $84 on Tuesday and $81 on Wednesday. Tuesday’s simple return is 84 ÷ 80 − 1 = 0.05 = 5%, while Wednesday’s is 81 ÷ 84 − 1 = −0.035714..., or about −3.57%; the denominator changes because each return uses the prior day’s price. If a quoted interest rate moves from 4.20% to 4.65%, the change is 0.45 percentage points, not 0.45%: the relative increase is 0.45 ÷ 4.20 ≈ 10.7%. A two-day price change can be computed from 81 ÷ 80 − 1 = 1.25%, but it hides the interim rise and fall. These transformations describe movement, not its cause or a reliable forecast. For a fuller treatment, see ‘FRED — What is FRED?’ in the linked sources.

Consider an illustrative synthetic investment with no interim cash flows and three consecutive simple returns: +5%, −4%, and +3%. Convert each percentage to a gross-return multiplier, 1.05, 0.96, and 1.03, then multiply rather than add: 1.05 × 0.96 = 1.008, and 1.008 × 1.03 = 1.03824. Thus $10,000 grows to $10,382.40, so the cumulative simple return is 1.03824 − 1 = 0.03824, or 3.824% (about 3.82%). The arithmetic average return is (5 − 4 + 3) ÷ 3 = 1.333% per period; it is a descriptive average, not the realized three-period return. Adding the three percentages would give 4%, overstating wealth because the −4% applies after the first gain and the +3% applies to the changing balance. This calculation assumes returns are measured on the same price basis and ignores fees, distributions, and timing within each period. If comparing assets, report both the horizon and compounding convention; otherwise a “3% return” can ambiguously mean one period, an average, or a cumulative result.
lessons.formula: Rₜ = Pₜ/Pₜ₋₁ − 1, where Pₜ is the current price and Pₜ₋₁ the prior price.
lessons.takeaway: Transformations change the question; label them and do not turn descriptive association into causal language.

practice.question: A price moves from 100 to 102. What is the simple return, and what unit should you use for a 0.50 yield move?
practice.hint: Divide the new price by the old price, and distinguish a rate level from a rate difference.
practice.solution: The return is 102/100 − 1 = 0.02 = 2%. A 0.50 move in a quoted yield is normally described as 0.50 percentage points, unless the source explicitly defines another unit.

lessons.title: Communicate uncertainty and practical importance
lessons.body:
A sample summary is uncertain because another defensible sample could differ. Standard error describes the repeated-sample variability of an estimator; it is not the same as the data's standard deviation. A confidence interval summarizes a method's long-run coverage under its assumptions, not a 95% probability attached to one fixed interval. Distinguish statistical evidence from effect size and practical importance: a tiny difference can be detectable in a huge sample, while an important difference can be imprecise in a small one. Association can support a prediction task, but causality needs design and assumptions. These are educational interpretations, not investment advice or a forecast.

Suppose an illustrative synthetic sample estimates an average monthly fee difference of $3.00 between two customer groups, with a 95% confidence interval from −$1.00 to $7.00 per customer per month. The interval’s width is $7 − (−1) = $8, so the estimate is not precise enough to rule out no difference or a modest negative difference under the stated method. If a business has pre-specified $10 per month as the threshold worth acting on, even the upper endpoint, $7, is below that practical threshold. A large sample could narrow the interval without making a $3 difference economically important; conversely, a small sample could leave a meaningful effect uncertain. This interval does not prove group membership causes fees, especially without random assignment. For a fuller treatment, see ‘Penn State STAT 200 — Descriptive Statistics’ in the linked sources.

Consider a new illustrative synthetic example: a researcher summarizes 36 monthly changes in a bond yield, measured in percentage points per month. The sample mean is 0.18 pp/month and the sample standard deviation is 0.60 pp/month. First compute the standard error: 0.60 / sqrt(36) = 0.60 / 6 = 0.10 pp/month. Using a 95% t interval with 35 degrees of freedom and t* ≈ 2.03, the margin of error is 2.03 × 0.10 = 0.203 pp/month, giving 0.18 ± 0.203 = [−0.023, 0.383], or about [−0.02, 0.38] pp/month after rounding. The interval includes zero, so the data do not clearly distinguish a positive average change from no average change under this method. It also spans a decision threshold of 0.25 pp/month: the estimate exceeds that threshold, but the uncertainty includes effects below it. This calculation treats the 36 months as a defensible target sample with sufficiently weak dependence and stable measurement; serial correlation, omitted months or regime shifts would make the standard error and interpretation unreliable. It describes an average change, not a policy effect or forecast.
lessons.takeaway: Report estimate, uncertainty, scale and design together; no single p-value or chart answers every question.

practice.question: A large sample finds a 0.01 percentage-point average yield difference with a narrow interval. Is it automatically important?
practice.hint: Compare the effect's units and consequences with a pre-specified meaningful threshold.
practice.solution: No. Statistical precision does not establish practical importance. Compare the interval and units with the decision threshold and consequences.

caseStudy: Imagine a risk analyst using FRED to obtain 10-year U.S. Treasury yields for a defined five-year window. The analyst computes daily changes, not just levels, with units in percentage points. A histogram and box plot show shape, median, quartiles, IQR, standard deviation and outliers; the 5th and 95th percentiles provide descriptive tail cutoffs. The analyst compares mean and median because a few shock days may pull the mean upward, then repeats the description at monthly frequency to show how aggregation changes the question. Any association between large moves and news periods remains descriptive: it does not prove a policy caused a move, predict the next move or establish economic importance. Missing dates, revisions, time-zone conventions, sample selection and changing regimes limit interpretation. The exercise uses observed-source data while numerical examples here are illustrative or simulated. It is a concise educational lesson in careful measurement and communication, not investment advice.
misconceptions: A large sample is automatically representative. Selection, nonresponse, survivorship and missing-period bias persist at any size.
The mean is always best, or the median is always better. The distribution, question, units and consequences determine the summary.
A percentile is a worst-case guarantee, or standard deviation is the probability of loss. Both depend on data and assumptions.
A trend, correlation or statistically detectable result proves causation or practical importance. Association, prediction, uncertainty and causality are distinct.

quiz.question: A few extreme daily yield changes make the mean jump, while the median barely moves. Which explanation is best?
options: The mean uses every value and is sensitive to extremes; the median depends on order.
The median is always the true population value.
The outliers must be measurement errors.
quiz.explanation: The mean uses every observed value and can be pulled by an extreme; the median depends on the ordered middle value(s), so one tail observation often moves it less.
